parsed.attack: The second photograph is a year away. A first-time rural owner does one adrenaline-fuelled sweep of the crawlspace in the week after completion - pressure tank, pump switch, softener, septic pump - and the inventory of a single house is finished in that one sitting; there is no third and no tenth item, because a house does not grow new equipment. The problem stops existing the moment the sweep is done, and the next genuine trigger is the next drip, which is measured in years, not weeks. The author's own kill line (under 30% photograph a second item within 7 days) will fail, and a $25 app opened once inside the refund window is exactly how you get an 8% refund rate.
parsed.strongest_defence: A one-time purchase does not need month-two usage to make money, and well-and-septic ownership generates a real recurring calendar that a suburban house does not - filter changes, pressure-switch cycling, tanks pumped every three to five years, and a fresh emergency every time the power cuts. The value is asymmetric and back-loaded by design: the sheet is worth nothing for eleven months and worth the whole $25 in the ten minutes you are standing in three inches of water reading a part number to a supplier, and the exported house sheet handed to a contractor or a buyer is the distribution loop rather than a retention mechanic.
parsed.verdict_reason: Usage genuinely collapses after one capture session, but the revenue is taken upfront and the artifact's value is real at a rare moment, so weak retention wounds the referral loop rather than the business.
